Q: Receive "Error reading input file" when running password decryption in BASH A:

I've tested your script, the error occurs because the file exists but contain bad ciphertext / does not match the decryption parameter. When the ciphertext matches, the script execute successfully.

Steps to test

  1. Save your bash script to file test.sh, add 2 lines at the bottom:
MASTER_PASSWORD='super_secret_master_password'
retrieve_password "$MASTER_PASSWORD"
  1. Generate the ciphertext using the exact parameter as the decryption command:
$ echo "test user password" > user.plain
$ openssl enc -e -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -a -iter 10000 \
  -pass "pass:super_secret_master_password" \
  -in user.plain \
  -out ./data/passwords/user
  1. Run the script
$ sh test.sh 
Please enter your account name: user
test user password
Please press Enter when done viewing ...

Q: Laravel Session Drivers? A:

Copied from the Laravel 13.x documentation.

The driver defines where session data will be stored.

file - sessions are stored in storage/framework/sessions.
cookie - sessions are stored in secure, encrypted cookies.
database - sessions are stored in a database (by default in the table sessions).
memcached / redis - sessions are stored in one of these fast, cache-based stores.
dynamodb - sessions are stored in AWS DynamoDB.
array - sessions are stored in a PHP array and will not be persisted1

native - Does not exist anymore since Laravel 5.

array driver means that session is only per request (stored during PHP runtime), and after that it disappears :)

1 (it's handled by MockArraySessionStorage).

Q: How do I serialize a floating point number? A:

IEEE754 is indeed pretty commonplace amongst today's CPUs. Not all CPUs exclusively use IEEE754; some have other representations to (e.g. POWER's decimal representation that is also on the chip as well as IEEE754), but it's been a long while since things other than IEEE754 looked like a good idea to chip designers. IBM's motivation for decimal as well as IEEE754 representations was to be good at financial calculations (where IEEE754 is not good enough), and they have a hardware co-processor for it.

Of course, whether or not serialising floating point data this way depends on application requirements. One of the obvious problems with just memcpying / casting a number to a byte array for storage is that one then has to have some way of indicating that this what's been done. There's nothing "automatic" about the representation that allows another program to independently work out that that's what the stored data is. Whether that matters or not is application specific.

There's been various attempts. For example, ASN.1 binary wireformats (e.g. BER) have two ways of serialising REALs. One is simply a text representation (even in a "binary" encoding such as BER, or the ultra-compact uPER). Another is a binary representation. The representation used depends on the value of the REAL, and choices made by the encoder which are likely influenced by the nature of the CPU it was written for. Semantically, a float in ASN.1-speak is an INTEGER mantissa, INTEGER base, and an INTEGER exponent. If the base is 10, text is used. If the base is 2, the encoding is binary, but that can be in encoded in 3 different bases (2, 8, 16), with a scale factor, sign flag, and any length of exponent and mantissa. Note that in ASN.1, INTEGERS are not bounded to anything so primitive as 64 bits, and for INTEGERs encoding switches between binary representations (which are used for 64bits or smaller) and text representations (for numbers > 64bits).

I think that most implementations just default to text for REALs regardless of value... However, that's an illustration of the kind of thing one has to do if one wants to be truly independent of how CPUs represent floating point values and avoid imposing limitations on precision within the representation. The complexity arising from the choices of encoding is supposedly worth it because it can adapt to whatever is good for the platform, an attribute likely pointless these days as IEEE754 is nearly good enough for everything (except money).

I like ASN.1, but it's not surprising that folk just byte-cast IEEE754 floats / doubles and leave it at that.

Q: _construct() is not called in class extending CI_Controller when instantiated in my CodeIgniter application A:

is your model file in models folder root? eg: application/models/administrator_model.php

or it is in a sub folder eg: application/models/admin/administrator_model.php then you have to load like $this->load->model('admin/administrator_model')

and the file name should be Ucfirst in CI3.0 but i forgot if it is necessary for CI2.2. (if you are using windows the filename wont bother until you deploy it to a linux server :)

Q: Is there a built-in function to print all the current properties and values of an object? A:

You can use the dir() function to do this. For example, to display the sys module:

>>> import sys
>>> dir(sys)
['__displayhook__', '__doc__', '__excepthook__', '__name__', '__stderr__', '__stdin__', '__stdo
t__', '_current_frames', '_getframe', 'api_version', 'argv', 'builtin_module_names', 'byteorder
, 'call_tracing', 'callstats', 'copyright', 'displayhook', 'dllhandle', 'exc_clear', 'exc_info'
 'exc_type', 'excepthook', 'exec_prefix', 'executable', 'exit', 'getcheckinterval', 'getdefault
ncoding', 'getfilesystemencoding', 'getrecursionlimit', 'getrefcount', 'getwindowsversion', 'he
version', 'maxint', 'maxunicode', 'meta_path', 'modules', 'path', 'path_hooks', 'path_importer_
ache', 'platform', 'prefix', 'ps1', 'ps2', 'setcheckinterval', 'setprofile', 'setrecursionlimit
, 'settrace', 'stderr', 'stdin', 'stdout', 'subversion', 'version', 'version_info', 'warnoption
', 'winver']
>>>

Another useful feature is help.

>>> help(sys)
Help on built-in module sys:

NAME
    sys

FILE
    (built-in)

MODULE DOCS
    http://www.python.org/doc/current/lib/module-sys.html

DESCRIPTION
    This module provides access to some objects used or maintained by the
    interpreter and to functions that interact strongly with the interpreter.

    Dynamic objects:

    argv -- command line arguments; argv[0] is the script pathname if known

Q: IF Reference Table contains Value1 or Value 2, then N, if not then Y A:

You don't say anything to indicate that it is important to retrieve the lookup values from the lists they are checked for in. It seems you only need to know they are present. Or not.

Using the lookup to find them would of course give them if found, or an error if not found. So one could do your lookup and use its result, comparing it to the lookup value to get a TRUE, and trap the error, if that happens, in a way to get a FALSE. But none of that is necessary.

You can use the following instead:

=IF(  SUM(  (A2 = D1:D20)*1,  (B2 = E1:E20)*1),  "No",  "Yes"  )

Each test in the SUM compares the appropriate lookup value to the ranges in question and gets an array of TRUE/FALSE values in return. Multiplying each array by "1" coerces that list into arrays of 1/0. Excel can add the values in those arrays via SUM, giving you a sum of all the results, and if that sum is anything, any value other than 0, Excel will treat it as TRUE. We think of it from the other direction: "TRUE = 1" but in truth, Excel regards any non-zero number as TRUE, not just 1. So 43876723 is TRUE, and so on. If neither value is in its lookup list, all the FALSE returns will coerce to being 0's and sum to 0. So now you have either a 1 or a 0 and IF can take the appropriate action.
